question: What are good practices for detecting AI-generated texts in situations where false positives are extremely expensive?

sections.title: Methodological Trade-offs
sections.text: Selecting an appropriate detection architecture is critical when computational resources and model access vary. Black-box approaches, including DetectGPT, NPR, and DNA-GPT, typically require multiple evaluations or generations, which results in significant computational overhead [1]. In contrast, white-box methods leverage model-internal metrics such as entropy, likelihood, and log-rank to assess text provenance [1]. While these internal signals can be informative, the high cost of black-box methods may limit their scalability in high-throughput environments where efficiency is a primary concern.

sections.title: Threshold-Free and Adaptive Architectures
sections.text: To mitigate the instability associated with fixed decision boundaries, adaptive frameworks have been developed to handle diverse text distributions. Agent-X is an adaptive guideline-based expert network designed for threshold-free AI-generated text detection, allowing the system to adapt its decision logic without relying on static cutoffs [1]. This approach is particularly relevant in scenarios where the distribution of human and machine-generated text shifts over time, as it avoids the brittleness inherent in threshold-based classifiers.

sections.title: Prioritizing False Positive Rates
sections.text: In contexts where false positives carry severe consequences, the evaluation metric must shift from general accuracy to specific error rates. For practical applications, it is essential to carefully evaluate detector effectiveness using the False Positive Rate (FPR) metric [2]. Systems that do not strictly adhere to low FPR criteria are not considered good or reliable for commercial applications, as they risk causing potential harm to users by incorrectly flagging human-authored content [2]. This standard is exemplified by Vietbinoculars, a zero-shot approach for detecting Vietnamese LLM-generated text, which prioritizes minimizing false alarms to ensure safety and reliability in deployment [2].

sections.title: Domain-Specific Challenges
sections.text: General-purpose detectors often fail when applied to specialized domains with unique stylistic constraints. Existing approaches for detecting AI text are poorly suited to the challenging problem of identifying AI-generated peer reviews, indicating a gap between general detection capabilities and domain-specific requirements [3]. This limitation suggests that good practices must include domain-specific validation and potentially the development of specialized models, rather than relying solely on generic detectors that may not account for the nuanced linguistic features of academic or professional writing.

question: What are good benchmarks and evaluation strategies for comparing obstacle avoidance strategies in mobile robots?

sections.title: Benchmark Selection and Task Suitability
sections.text: Obstacle avoidance is a suitable benchmark task for mobile robots because it can be implemented with varying numbers of robots and relies on basic sensors and actuators available in most platforms [5]. This task allows for the definition of clear performance metrics and serves as a standard for testing learning algorithms [5]. Historically, obstacle avoidance was utilized in some of the earliest works applying Genetic Algorithms to real robots for evaluative adaptation, and it has also been employed to test other learning methods such as Particle Swarm optimization [5]. The strategy encompasses a variety of methods, including behavior learning. While global path planning focuses on static scenes and requires full knowledge of the environment to search for a target from an initial location [4] [2], reactive approaches often lack memory, can be overly cautious, and perform poorly in challenging conditions. To address these limitations, hybrid navigation methods have been proposed that combine global path planning with reactive methods to guarantee safe navigation in partially known, dynamic environments [3]. This hybrid approach aims to provide an optimal solution by leveraging the benefits of both global and reactive navigation to overcome the constraints of relying primarily on one method [3]. Additionally, reactive obstacle-avoidance systems for wheeled mobile robots based on artificial intelligence have been presented [2], and several algorithms have been proposed, each possessing specific drawbacks and benefits [1]. Other strategies include those based on wireless sensor networks for real-time performance and accuracy , as well as ant colony algorithms inspired by biological technology for path planning.

sections.title: Mixed-Initiative and Interactive Clarification
sections.text: A key challenge in automation is detecting and balancing when to automate grounding decisions versus when to require explicit user consultation [5]. Irresolvable ambiguities should be handled through mixed-initiative specification, which cooperatively engages the user to resolve issues rather than failing or guessing [5]. Systems like MISP and DialSQL employ a mixed-initiative approach by asking follow-up questions to clarify user intent, such as distinguishing between 'sales amount' and 'number of sales' [4]. These interactive methods help establish 'common ground' between the user and the AI [4]. However, users can become frustrated if the conversation becomes repetitive or fails to address the core error [4]. In text-to-SQL contexts, question rewriting has emerged as an effective strategy to address ambiguity in natural language questions [3].

question: What are leading methods for generating hard examples of the boolean satisfiability problem, and what are their strengths and weaknesses?

sections.title: Problem Definition and Complexity
sections.text: The Boolean satisfiability problem (SAT) is a well-known NP-hard problem with significant practical applications [9]. It involves determining whether truth values can be assigned to Boolean variables in a propositional formula such that the overall expression evaluates to true [8]. Alternatively, it can be framed as finding an assignment that maximizes the number of satisfied clauses in a given set of constraints [7]. SAT solvers are programs designed to automatically solve these problems [6]. Although the problem is old, designing efficient methods remains an active area of research [5]. Results from SAT and constraint satisfaction (CP) have had a major impact on developing fast and robust solvers, significantly expanding their range of effectiveness [4]. The complexity of variants like Unique k-SAT, where the promise is that there is at most one solution, remains unresolved, specifically whether it is P^NP-complete [3]. However, evidence suggests Unique k-SAT is as hard to solve as general k-SAT [2]. Valiant and Vazirani provided a randomized polynomial time reduction from SAT to Unique SAT, demonstrating that deciding whether a CNF formula has zero or one solution is essentially as difficult as SAT in general [1][1]. The PPSZ algorithm exhibits a gap between k-SAT and unique k-SAT, as it has been derandomized for unique k-SAT but not for the general case.

sections.title: Random Instance Generation Models
sections.text: Models for generating random instances of search problems have received much attention from the artificial intelligence community over the last twenty years [4]. These models often reveal an intriguing phase-transition phenomenon [4][4]. A 2018 paper proposed new models for generating hard random Boolean formulas and disjunctive logic programs [4]. Specifically, it introduced three models: a multi-component model consisting of disjunctions of t CNF formulas, a fixed-length clause model, and a controlled model [4]. These were compared to the Chen-Interian and Navarro-Voronkov fixed-shape models [4]. In the multi-component model, where t is fixed, the probability of satisfiability is not affected by whether the disjunction is interpreted as a set or an ordered list [4]. If the limit of t^2/N as N approaches infinity is 0, there exists a sequence epsilon_N such that the limit of epsilon_N is 0, and the probability p_N is bounded by p_N' within epsilon_N [4]. The multi-component model allows for hardness control via the parameter t [4]. The controlled model generates harder instances than the Chen-Interian model [4].

sections.text: The evaluation of complex scientific question answering (QA) has evolved from rudimentary rule-based systems to modern deep learning architectures and large pre-trained models [5]. Knowledge-based QA remains a challenging NLP task, with mainstream approaches divided into semantic parsing, information extraction, and retrieval-based categories [4]. Applying large language models (LLMs) to scientific domains is particularly difficult due to the unique characteristics of scientific language and knowledge [3]. While existing work often evaluates models under single-constraint settings like formality, complex scientific QA requires assessing deeper context understanding [2]. Historical comparisons of major QA systems have focused on statistical approaches and their performance metrics [1].

sections.title: Reproducibility and Modular Frameworks
sections.text: A significant barrier in open-domain QA is the difficulty of reproducing results due to complex configurations and high resource requirements [6]. The SF-QA framework addresses this by modularizing the open-domain QA pipeline, making the task accessible and reproducible for research groups with limited computing resources [6]. It ensures consistency by recording parameter settings for different models in separate configuration files, allowing existing models to be directly reused [6]. This modular approach contrasts with the resource-intensive nature of building full systems from scratch [6].

snippets: it requires large amounts of resources for building the full system and it is often difficult to reproduce previous results due to complex configurations

Moreover, parameter settings for different models are recorded and saved in another separate configuration file, as shown in the section 3.6 . Therefore, any existing models in the current SF-QA project can be directly reproduced, which would greatly facilitate researchers in establishing benchmark scores and doing fair comparisons.

In this paper, we introduce SF-QA: simple and fair evaluation framework for open-domain QA. SF-QA framework modularizes the pipeline open-domain QA system, which makes the task itself easily accessible and reproducible to research groups without enough computing resources.

sections.title: Scientific Context and Heterogeneous Data
sections.text: Recent benchmarks emphasize the need to evaluate LLMs on noisy, lengthy, and heterogeneous scientific contexts, including text, relational graphs, and tabular data, rather than just direct QA tasks [3]. SciCUEval is a comprehensive dataset designed for this purpose, consisting of 10 sub-datasets (2 unstructured text, 4 structured table, and 4 other), with 90.83% of instances meeting high-quality criteria [3]. It assesses four competencies, including Relevant Information Identification, which distinguishes relevant data from extraneous noise [3]. Performance varies by format; for instance, one model achieved 71.91 on text, 55.91 on tables, 63.13 on knowledge graphs, and an overall score of 61.52 [3]. Another model recorded 72.22 on text and 42.98 on tables. Other datasets include sciverse_ccsbench, arxiv_2101.01910 (SF-QA), sciverse_testing_qa_software, and sciverse_scirag.

sections.title: Domain-Specific and Multi-Disciplinary Benchmarks
sections.text: Evaluation is expanding into specific scientific fields. MatSciBench contains 1,340 college-level materials science problems across 6 primary fields and 31 sub-fields, using a 3-tier difficulty scale; Gemini-2.5-Pro achieved less than 80% accuracy. WildSci provides domain-specific questions from peer-reviewed literature across 9 disciplines and 26 subdomains in a multiple-choice format suitable for reinforcement learning. SCI-VerifyBench covers math, physics, biology, and chemistry to address the lack of systematic evaluation standards. PAPERMIND evaluates agent-oriented scientific reasoning over research papers across 7 domains and 4 task families, focusing on grounding and cross-source synthesis. Financial QA datasets include ConvFinQA (14,115 examples), PACIFIC (19,008 examples), TAT-DQA (16,558 examples), and MMQA (29,918 examples). A broader taxonomy includes MRQA (SQuAD 1.1, NewsQA, TriviaQA, SearchQA), Open-Domain (Natural Questions, Web Questions), and Multi-Choice (CommonsenseQA, OpenBookQA, CosmosQA) benchmarks.

sections.title: Advanced Evaluation Methodologies
sections.text: Newer methodologies focus on automated generation and agentic workflows. CQ^2A leverages LLMs to generate questions from context and answers, extracting entities and relationships to enhance the completeness and naturalness of QA testing [7]. However, this approach faces challenges with hallucinations, where generated questions may introduce information not present in the source or violate prompt constraints [7]. JudgeFlow optimizes agentic workflows using block judges to provide fine-grained diagnostic signals for LLM-based processes. Qworld uses recursive expansion trees to create question-specific evaluation criteria, covering 89% of expert criteria and generating 79% novel criteria on HealthBench. Deep Data Research introduces DDR-Bench, a checklist-based benchmark for verifiable evaluation of autonomous insight extraction, distinguishing investigatory from executional intelligence. Additionally, LLM-as-judge frameworks can fail when reference answers conflict with the judge's parametric knowledge, a flaw revealed by swapped-reference QA tests. Multi-hop QA evaluation focuses on reasoning across snippets, relevance, and fluency, while DROP uses 9,536 examples with few-shot settings and F1 score metrics. CCSBench reports inter-annotator agreement greater than 0.85 and accuracy scores above 0.9. Deep Research unifies industry applications and AI for Science as a prototypical vertical app for general-purpose agents.

In this study, we leverage the strong text generation capabilities of LLMs to generate questions given a specific context and answer.
Distinct from existing test generation approaches, $CQ^2 A$ extracts entities/relationships from the context to serve as answers, and subsequently generates corresponding questions.
As a result, $CQ^2 A$ significantly enhances both the completeness and naturalness of testing for QA systems.
